source_refs.note: 3. Veins: a main subheading of 11.2 Blood vessels, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 243-244.

blocks.text: These blood vessels carry blood from different parts of the body towards heart. All veins carry deoxygenated blood, except pulmonary veins. The wall of veins has same three layers as are present in arteries. The outer layer i.e., tunica externa (adventitia) is made of connective and elastic tissue. The middle layer i.e., tunica media is relatively thin and only slightly muscular, with few elastic fibres. The inner layer i.e., tunica intima is made of thin layer of endothelial cells.

blocks.alt: A cut-away vein as stepped cylinders: a wide lumen with a valve inside it, lined by the tunica intima (endothelium); a thin tunica media of smooth muscles; and the outer tunica externa, with a venule joining from the side.
blocks.caption: Figure 11.8: Structure of vein (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 11.8).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Valve, Tunica intima (endothelium), Lumen, Smooth muscles, Tunica media, Tunica externa, Venule.

blocks.text: The middle layer of veins is relatively thinner than that of arteries because veins do not have to withstand high blood pressure. An empty artery is still a hollow tube but an empty vein collapses like an empty balloon. Semilunar valves are present in veins to prevent the back flow of blood, as it is moving towards heart. The pressure generated by the contraction of surrounding muscles presses veins and assists in the return of blood towards heart.

Smaller veins join to form larger veins and ultimately from vena cavae (inferior vena cava and superior vena cava), which pour blood into the right atrium of heart. Pulmonary veins from lungs empty in left atrium.

blocks.alt: A red artery on the left gives off arterioles; at the entry of each capillary loop is a precapillary sphincter. Purple capillaries join the arterioles to venules, which open into a blue vein on the right.
blocks.caption: Figure 11.9: Relationship of arterioles, capillaries & venules (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 11.9).
